name: Rebuild a tree from its saved text
brief:
A pricing service saves its decision tree as text. It writes the tree in preorder, node first, then the left part, then the right part, and writes `#` for each empty tree. Tokens are separated by spaces or line breaks, and a value is a whole number that may be negative. Rebuild the tree as a nested tuple `(value, left, right)`, with `None` for an empty tree.

Write `read_tree(text)`.

Example. `"5 3 # # 8 # #"` holds 5, then its left part `3 # #`, then its right part `8 # #`. So the answer is `(5, (3, None, None), (8, None, None))`.
constraints: At most $100{,}000$ values, in a tree of height at most 400. The text is a whole, well-formed tree; `"#"` alone is the empty tree.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Split the text into tokens and read them with one moving position. Reading a tree means: take a token; if it is `#` the tree is empty, otherwise read the left tree, then the right tree.

examples.note: Each leaf is followed by two `#` marks, one for each empty side.
The first `#` is the empty left side of -12, and 40 is its right child.

tests.expect: (1, (2, (4, None, None), None), (3, None, (5, None, None)))

tests.call: read_tree(' '.join(['1'] * 400 + ['#'] * 401)) == __import__('functools').reduce(lambda t, v: (1, t, None), range(400), None)

read_tree(' '.join((lambda f: f(f, 0, 65535))(lambda f, lo, hi: ['#'] if lo >= hi else [str((lo + hi) // 2 - 30000)] + f(f, lo, (lo + hi) // 2) + f(f, (lo + hi) // 2 + 1, hi)))) == (lambda f: f(f, 0, 65535))(lambda f, lo, hi: None if lo >= hi else ((lo + hi) // 2 - 30000, f(f, lo, (lo + hi) // 2), f(f, (lo + hi) // 2 + 1, hi)))

read_tree('\n'.join((lambda f: f(f, 0, 100000))(lambda f, lo, hi: ['#'] if lo >= hi else [str(lo * 7 - hi)] + f(f, lo, (lo + hi) // 2) + f(f, (lo + hi) // 2 + 1, hi)))) == (lambda f: f(f, 0, 100000))(lambda f, lo, hi: None if lo >= hi else (lo * 7 - hi, f(f, lo, (lo + hi) // 2), f(f, (lo + hi) // 2 + 1, hi)))

how: Submit runs 12 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value.
notes: Preorder with a mark for every empty side fixes the shape, so one left-to-right read rebuilds it.
Reading one character at a time breaks values such as `-12` and `100`.
Each token is read once, so the work is $O(n)$.

planted.slip: Reading one character at a time splits `-12` and `100` into separate tokens.
Reading the right part first hangs every left subtree on the right.
Splitting on a single space leaves empty tokens where spaces repeat, and misses line breaks.
